sources.news_title: UK Suspects Iran Involved in Incident at Air Base Housing US Forces
sources.text:
The UK believes Iran played a part in a suspected terrorist plot last weekend at an airbase in England used by the U.S. Air Force, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Sept. 30.
“There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford,” Burnham told the BBC Wednesday.
The prime minister said the complex and serious police investigation into the incident that involved the arrest of five British citizens was ongoing.
Gloucestershire police and British counter terrorism detectives were working with U.S. colleagues on the case, according to the prime minister.
“We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran played a part,” Burnham said.
National Counter Terrorism Policing detectives were tipped off about three vans that were seen heading toward the military airfield Sunday, the agency reported Tuesday.
The base has been the site of protests by anti-war activists in the past and used by Americans for decades, including during this year’s conflict with Iran.
Five British men were arrested near the base Sunday night and faced explosives and terror charges. The men, who haven’t been publicly identified by the police, were released on bail Monday.
Detectives searched the vans driven by the suspects. No bombs were located, but they did find flammable materials, National Counter Terrorism Policing said.
“Those vehicles have been subject to extensive examination, with the support of military assets and forensic experts, and we can confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found,” the agency stated. “However, a quantity of petrol was recovered.”
The suspects were released but are still under investigation and must adhere to strict conditions, according to police.
UK authorities said the men were British nationals from London in their 20s.
The female farmer who called in the tip to authorities Sunday spoke with an independent news reporter about the sighting. She said she witnessed a “large group of men” who started to run into a field toward the air base, noting there were more than five and may have been as many as 10 in the group that were dressed the same and had their faces covered.
Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps said in July that RAF Fairford was one of several airbases in the UK that were legitimate targets.
The Iranian Embassy in the UK released a statement rejecting the reports by media and British officials linking Iran to the five arrested in the RAF Fairford base incident.
“The Islamic Republic of Iran reserves the right to take appropriate legal measures, as necessary, to safeguard the rights and interests of the country and its people in response to misleading and damaging media narratives,” the embassy posted on X.

UK PM says 'strong indications' Iran involved in airbase incident
London (AFP) – British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Wednesday said there were "strong indications" Iran was involved in suspicious activity at a UK airbase that triggered a major security incident this weekend.
Issued on:
"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford," Burnham told the BBC, referring to Sunday's bomb scare near the airbase in southwest England, which is used by the US military in its war against Iran.
"Of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation," said Burnham.
Iran's embassy in London earlier said it "categorically rejects and strongly condemns" speculation it was involved in the incident, while Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi posted on X that Burnham was "barking up the wrong tree".
Police said on Tuesday that no explosives were found at the scene. The nature of the threat has not been explained by officials.
Burnham's comments are the first official confirmation from UK authorities that Iran may have had a hand in the incident, which saw three white vans appearing to head towards RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday.
A local resident who rang the police said she saw a group of masked men near the vans, which were blocking a road in a village next to the military base.
Growing confusion
The case was plunged into confusion when UK police released on bail five British men it had arrested on Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences.
After three days of investigations, including using a bomb disposal team, police said Tuesday they had found no explosives in the vehicles, but they had retrieved a "quantity of petrol".
Then on Wednesday, The Times newspaper reported that the incident had been foiled after one of the five suspects tipped off the police before the group was apprehended.
US President Donald Trump and his Secretary of State Marco Rubio had previously indicated that intelligence bodies were aware of the suspects and that a foreign state could be involved, but UK officials had not weighed in.
"We have been waiting to confirm what we could say, but we can now confirm our belief that Iran played a part," Burnham told Sky News.
Speculation was rife that Iran or another hostile state could have been involved, after Tehran previously warned London against allowing its military bases to be used by Washington.
Britain gave the US the greenlight to use RAF Fairford for defensive strikes against Iran, drawing Tehran's ire and unease from some residents in the Gloucestershire countryside where the base is located.

sources.news_title: Why British PM Andy Burnham named Iran as likely culprit in air base plot
sources.text:
Why British PM named Iran as likely culprit in air base plot
London: Political leaders are often wary of naming the culprit behind a security alert even when their officials quietly brief the media about threats from state spy agencies.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham set aside that standard caution on Wednesday by naming Iran as a likely player in the alarming plot against a Royal Air Force base in the early hours of Sunday morning.
Burnham made a calculated decision to go public with the assessment from intelligence agencies about the threat to the Fairford air force base when he sat down for a scheduled interview with the BBC.
“There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course, it remains an ongoing, complex and serious police investigation,” he said.
“And, of course, we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America.
“We are on top of it in every possible way imaginable. Police in Gloucestershire [and] our Counter Terrorism Police have done an outstanding job. I thank them for that.
“We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part.”
All the signs point to an Iranian ploy to hire small-time criminals to test the defences at a major base – in this case, a base used to support American bombers that strike Iranian targets.
Five men were arrested in the early hours of Sunday near the base with three vans thought to carry explosives.
Police have since stated that they did not find any explosives, although they did find stored fuel.
While this led to online theories that the suspects were merely stealing fuel from nearby farms, that idea flies in the face of the reality. The suspects appeared to be testing the defences of a major military base, without going so far as to launch an attack.
In naming Iran, the prime minister put paid to the theory that the suspects were in the area for some minor reason.
The fact that the police released the five suspects on bail also tends to support the idea that the men were minor criminals. The logical objective is to keep them under surveillance rather than in detention.
One key fact remains a source of mystery. The Times of London revealed that one of the suspects called the 999 emergency phone line – the UK equivalent of triple zero – to notify the police of the activities near the base.
The suspect made this call at 12.45am, the BBC reported. This was before a local farmer saw the men and called police after 1.30am. London’s The Telegraph reported that a suspect made the first call to authorities.
The Iranian ambassador in London has denied any Iranian responsibility for the plot, but that can be taken with a grain of salt.
Political leaders and national security agencies have been wary in the past about naming the source of a threat. Burnham’s remarks are a sign that he puts a greater priority on being frank with citizens about the scale of the dangers from state threats. His predecessor, Keir Starmer, was by nature more cautious.
Burnham is not alone in this approach. When German authorities detected a drone attack on an aircraft at Leipzig in early August, it began an investigation and later named Russia as the instigator.
In short, governments of all kinds are now being more assertive about naming culprits.
Burnham’s comments bring the public position in London closer to the line taken in Washington, DC after US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, said the incident “clearly involves” a foreign actor.
There is still a gulf, however, between the UK government and the American president, Donald Trump, on what has gone on. Trump said authorities had the five suspects under surveillance for a long time. No UK minister or security official has said the same thing.
Australians will recognise the careful language Burnham used to attribute blame without being definitive. When Jewish community sites were attacked in Sydney and Melbourne in late 2024, authorities took time to determine the ultimate source of the danger.

Wednesday saw Prime Minister Andy Burnham finally make an open suggestion that Iran was implicated in events that led to the arrest of five men near Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford in Gloucestershire, England.
Speaking after the end of the Labour Party conference on a terror investigation ongoing since Sunday, Burnham told the BBC, “There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation.
“And of course, we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America. So it’s ongoing.”
“We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part,” he continued.
The arrests in the early hours of Sunday morning unleashed immediate speculation of a bomb plot targeting the base from which US planes have taken off on bombing sorties against Iran. But events over the following days saw revelations that threw a question mark over heavy suggestions of Iranian involvement, and even over whether there was any terror incident to be involved in.
The suspects were initially detained under the Explosives Act and later under Section 5 of the Terrorism Act. US President Donald Trump immediately stoked a media firestorm by declaring Sunday that the men had been intending to carry out a “terror plot” and “looking to do big damage”. Speaking to reporters, Trump stated that the US had been “working with Britain” and “had them under view for a long time and we got them.”
On Monday, UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters the UK would not be “cowed by sabre-rattling from Iran” or allow the country to “dictate our foreign policy”. That evening, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio declared that the event in Fairford “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor” and thanked the UK for being cooperative.
However, from the night the arrests took place the police’s own actions and the official statements of both the police and the UK government were blowing holes in the narrative presented by the US government.
The initial report was that a farmer had encountered three white vans blocking a road near Fairford. Having turned around, she says she saw a large group of hooded and masked men (more than five) near a junction. They dispersed after seeing her.
The woman attempted to contact the Ministry of Defence Police, receiving no answer, before calling Gloucestershire police on 999 at 1:36 a.m. to report suspicious activity.
Armed police supported by a helicopter arrived 10 minutes later, arresting five men 300 metres from the Fairford perimeter. The local area was declared the scene of a major incident, with over 80 households evacuated while army bomb disposal personnel examined the three vans using robots.
Later that day, British police and intelligence sources suggested that the specific activities of the arrested men were not necessarily known to the authorities, as Trump’s remarks implied. However, Counter Terror Police took over the investigation, stating that they were investigating whether those involved “might have been acting knowingly or unknowingly on behalf of a foreign state”.
The official position of the emergency government Cobra meetings held Sunday and Monday was that the investigation was live but it was too early to establish attribution.
At 4 p.m. on Monday, police then made the extraordinary announcement that all five men would be released on police bail, under stringent conditions but without charge. Terror suspects can be held for up to 14 days. The action was described as an “investigative” decision “grounded in experience and careful considerations of policing powers”.
This confirmed that no physical evidence of a bomb plot had been found.
A former head of the UK’s National Counter Terrorism Security Office, Chris Phillips, told Al Jazeera, “If there had been any trace of explosives found in the vans, or any thoughts that these men were actually terrorists, they would not have been released.”
The three vans, it was revealed, carried only plastic barrels, with one containing “a quantity of petrol”. All the vehicles displayed a counterfeit red logo reading “Fuel2You”. Police said they could “confirm that no improvised explosive devices were found.”
Phillips added that a terror investigation would have meant keeping the suspects held in custody to “go through all their records and all their contacts and what they’ve been doing and what they’ve been talking about.” No information has been released about the five arrestees, other than that they are all from men from London in their 20s.
Just as suspiciously, it was revealed Tuesday that one of the arrested men had himself called the police at 12:45 a.m. Sunday morning, almost an hour before the farmer’s call to Gloucestershire police.
These facts led to widespread suggestions that a gang of fuel thieves, not terrorists, had been caught. Afzal Ashraf, visiting fellow in international relations and security at Loughborough University and a former senior Royal Air Force officer, told Al Jazeera that the local area had many houses reliant on heating oil stored in tanks.
“When you’ve got several hundred litres in gardens, that’s a bit of a killing for somebody,” he said, calling this “an alternative and probably more plausible explanation” than a terror plot. “There’s absolutely nothing else at all, at the moment, suggesting that there is a link to any foreign government,” he added.
Trump responded angrily to the release of the five: “I would have said ‘Don’t let them have bail’. I’m surprised that they released them. I wouldn’t have done that.” Asked by reporters whether he thought the incident had a connection with Iran, he replied, “It might,” declining to elaborate but claiming he knew the answer. Rubio also stated that “there was a lot more news to come” and stressed US concerns at the release of the five men.
Trump smugly declared of the five men at one point, “We know everything about them.” But to date, neither Trump nor Rubio has explicitly accused Iran of responsibility.
The Iranian Embassy in the UK responded by saying it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations published by some British individuals and media outlets attempting to link Iran to the arrest of five suspects in the vicinity of RAF Fairford base.”
Newsweek senior editor Shane Croucher gave a shrewd analysis of the Trump administration’s motivation behind aggressively suggesting Iranian involvement, writing that the Fairford incident “might be just the incident president Donald Trump has needed after months of frustration with NATO allies.
“In March, after European allies rebuffed his request for help reopening the Strait of Hormuz… Fairford now offers a test closer to the alliance’s purpose—defending an ally’s own soil.”
Burnham’s latest statement, though still cautious, indicates that Britain is now adopting the Iranian terror narrative, telling the BBC that he couldn’t “go into all of those details” regarding Iranian involvement, “but obviously I wouldn’t say it lightly.”

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham: ‘Strong indications’ Iran played a role in RAF Fairford incident
sources.text:
Iran is likely to have played a role in the suspected terror plot outside RAF Fairford, the prime minister has said.
Five men, all British nationals in their 20s, were arrested near the RAF base, which is also used by the United States in Gloucestershire on Sunday.
Earlier this week, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio suggested “a foreign actor” may have had involvement in the incident.
In interviews broadcast today, Andy Burnham said that it seemed likely that Iran had a role.
He told the BBC’s Chris Mason: “There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation.
“And of course, we are working closely with our colleagues in the United States of America.”
He also noted that he held a Cobra meeting on the incident on Monday, while at the Labour Party’s annual conference in Liverpool.
The prime minister sought to reassure viewers by saying that the government were “on top of it in every possible way imaginable”.
He continued: “Police in Gloucestershire, our counter-terrorism police have done an outstanding job. I thank them for that. We will say more in due course, but we can confirm our belief that we believe Iran to have played a part.”
Pressed by Mason on what led the government to believe Iranian involvement, Burnham replied that he “can't go into all of those details, but obviously I wouldn't say it lightly”.
On Monday, Donald Trump expressed criticism of the decision of authorities to grant bail to the suspects arrested in Gloucestershire, telling reporters: "I wouldn't have done that”.
Asked about Trump’s comments and whether British authorities had a grip on the situation, Burnham replied that the suspects had been released “obviously with the strictest possible bail conditions.”
He added: “We've been talking to counterparts in the United States all week to explain what is happening here, how things are being done, I have complete confidence in the way British security services are handling this.”
In a different interview, with GB News’ Christopher Hope, he alluded to the depth of cooperation with the US: “It's obviously a very serious investigation involving our colleagues in the United States, and we are working very closely with them. And I will say more when I can.”
However, asked by Channel 5’s Andy Bell, the prime minister refused to be drawn on whether the use of RAF Fairford by the United States – including to bomb targets in Iran – invited a greater security threat onto Britain.
“It's too early to jump to conclusions. It is an ongoing investigation and it's a very serious one.
“As I just said, all of that is being looked at, motive and of course what happened on the night.
“And we're grateful to the member of the public for ringing the alarm, but also our police in Gloucestershire. Our security services have done an outstanding job. We're grateful to them but we will say more when we can”, he told the broadcaster.”

UK's Burnham cites 'strong indications' Iran linked to suspected plot near US-used airbase
(TNND) — British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Wednesday there are “strong indications” that Iran played a part in a suspected terrorist plot near RAF Fairford, a U.S.-used airbase in England.
“There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation,” Burnham told the BBC.
Burnham said the U.K. is working closely with U.S. officials and would provide more information “in due course.”
His comments follow Secretary of State Marco Rubio’s statement Tuesday that the incident “clearly involves the hands of a foreign actor.” Trump had earlier said the suspects “might be” connected to Iran.
Iran’s Embassy in London on Monday denied any role in the incident, calling speculation linking Tehran to the five suspects “unfounded and malicious.” The embassy said the claims would fuel “Iranophobia propaganda” in the U.K. and that Iran reserved the right to pursue legal action over what it called misleading media narratives.
Metropolitan Police said officers detained the men Sunday after receiving a call from a nearby farmer about three suspicious vehicles that appeared to be traveling toward the Gloucestershire base.
British media reported Wednesday that one of the five suspects called 999, Britain’s emergency number, shortly before the arrests.
The Times and BBC reported that the call came nearly an hour before a local farmer reported seeing masked men and three white vans near RAF Fairford. The Times reported officers were already at the scene when the farmer made the later call and said investigators were examining why the suspect contacted police.
Police have said more than one piece of information prompted their response. “A police response was activated in the early hours of Sunday morning due to a range of information received, including a call from a member of the public about several vehicles acting suspiciously close to RAF Fairford,” Assistant Commissioner Laurence Taylor said.
The five men — all British nationals and London residents aged 23 to 25 — were arrested on suspicion of offenses under the Explosives Act and preparation of a terrorist act, police said.
Taylor said officers found “no improvised explosive devices” in the vehicles, though "a quantity of petrol was recovered."
The men were released on bail while the counterterrorism investigation continues, according to officials. No charges have been announced, and police have not publicly detailed the evidence behind the government’s assessment of Iranian involvement.
“To be very clear, this does not mean the investigation is over,” Taylor said. “They are subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others.”
Trump said during an announcement about a steel plant in Iowa that he was “surprised” British authorities released the suspects on bail, telling reporters in the Oval Office: “I wouldn’t have done that.”
RAF Fairford has been used by American bombers for strictly limited strikes against Iran under an agreement with former British Prime Minister Keir Starmer, who has voiced opposition to the war.

LONDON, Sept 30 (Reuters) - Britain has "strong indications" that Iran was involved in a suspected plot against a British airbase used by US forces to strike Iran, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said on Wednesday.
In an incident which triggered a huge police response, raised alarm among Western allies, and remains largely unexplained, five British men in their 20s were arrested on Sunday on suspected terrorism and explosive offences near RAF Fairford in western England.
The five, who all live in London, were later released on bail.
"There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford, but of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation," Burnham told the BBC in an interview.
On Monday, Iran strongly denied any involvement, responding to reports that it could be involved in the incident.
Burnham said Britain was working closely with the US, whose bombers have in recent months used the base to launch missions against Iran.
Shortly after the arrests, President Donald Trump said the men had planned "big damage" and his Secretary of State Marco Rubio later pointed at "a foreign actor".
Until Burnham's remarks, Britain had not linked the incident to Iran, though counter-terrorism police have said their investigation included the possibility of foreign state involvement and whether the incident could involve proxies "knowingly or unknowingly working on behalf of a foreign state".

sources.news_title: Andy Burnham tells GB News 'strong indications' Iran was behind RAF Fairford incident
sources.text:
Prime Minister Andy Burnham has told GB News that there are “strong indications” that Iran was behind the recent security alert at RAF Fairford.
In an interview with GB News Political Editor Christopher Hope, he also denied that he had changed his view on Brexit and dismissed a suggestion that Labour was unfairly targeting pensioners.
On RAF Fairford, he said: “So what I can say is there are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend. It is, though, still an ongoing and very serious police investigation. So, I hope you’ll understand if I don’t say more at this point.
“I wanted to confirm what we could say. But this will continue now. It’s obviously a very serious investigation involving our colleagues in the United States, and we are working very closely with them, and I will say more when I can.
“Obviously, I’ve been dealing with this as I’ve been here in Liverpool. We have held a Cobra meeting here during the week. We are completely on top of things, but we will say more when we can.”
Asked if he had changed his view on Brexit: “I certainly haven’t gone back – no, because I said very clearly in the speech and afterwards, we look at all options. The speech was about deciding the long-term direction for this country. Where do we want to be in 10 years’ time? And I don’t think we now can leave that question unanswered.
“An option is to stay as we are. Of course, that’s an option. Quite clearly, that’s an option. But public opinion has shifted in that decade, including in Makerfield. And it’s right that I say, ‘Well, here are the options’. George Osborne’s put an option forward. Canada has talked about a different relationship with the European Union. I can’t leave Britain out of those discussions.
“We do have to have an honest and grown-up conversation about well, what could a future relationship look like, and then come back to the public and say, well, here are the broad options and here are the issues involved with each of them. That’s just the right way to lead. I’ve got to do what’s best for this country.”
Asked if re-joining the EU was an option, Burnham said: “Well, people look at all the options, and where is the centre of gravity? Is there a new centre of gravity? If there’s not a consensus, that would also inform my thinking. My job is to secure the best interests of this country. That’s what I was talking about yesterday, and you know I’m going to take on issues, even if they’re politically difficult, to do what’s right for Britain. That’s what I’m going to do.
“The decade we’ve just been through has not been good enough. I don’t think Brexit has helped us. If I’m honest, I think it has caused harm. So the question is, we can’t have another decade like the one we’ve just had. So what are we going to do in this next decade? And that’s what I was addressing directly in my speech yesterday, and more honestly, perhaps, than sometimes these things have been done in the past.”
On immigration, he said: “Now, one thing that I want to convey here is Brexit has changed the nature of immigration to this country, because in the past, when we were in the European Union, people can have their view about it, about whether it was good or bad, but what we had was a more revolving door form of migration, where people would come here in their younger years. Many people did from Eastern Europe, people would remember, and they’d maybe spend you know a few years here in their mid to late 20s, and then go home and start a family. And that was a very common form of immigration.
“Now, immigration is more likely to be a permanent settlement where people are coming on a visa to work here. And then we saw obviously the Boris wave and the changes that came through in that in that period. So it’s changed the nature of immigration.
“But the second thing about control, if I could just say this: when we left, we lost access to the crucial immigration database held across Europe, which tells you where people arrived and what countries they’ve been through, and that is information that is invaluable when it comes to managing migration.
“So, you know, I think it’s important now that we put these more you know nuanced issues on the table, so people can make their own judgment in the round of whether Brexit’s been a good or a bad thing.”
Asked if he was being tone deaf to the concerns of people in his own constituency, he said: “No, it’s not, because we are the government that’s got small boat crossings down significantly down, down this year on last year, and down by around a half on the early 2020s. So where the other government talked tough and didn’t do anything, we’ve done it. And credit to the Home Secretary for the way she’s got a grip on these things.
“In terms of HMO Britain, yes, I did call that out. Why? Because we’ve had an approach in the past of the poorest communities being asked to deal with the whole issue of asylum accommodation, and that just simply isn’t fair. So it does pass the Makerfield test. Indeed, it does, for me to say to you that that can’t continue where places like Makerfield and all of the towns within it are the places where the authorities only look to deal with this whole question of asylum accommodation.
“Well, as I say, I live on the edge of the Makerfield constituency, so no one is saying, “Oh, it’s different rules for me and not for others’. But I accept that the situation with a barracks is a different situation than an HMO or a more dispersed model, or even the hotels.
“I think people wanted us to move people out of hotels. That was a very clear call of a few years ago, and that explains now why the barracks option is being looked at. But I’ve heard what people are saying in Piddington and the other places affected. I don’t ignore their concerns. Of course, they’re raising concerns that need to be looked at, and I will as and when any plans are taken forward.”
On changes to the triple lock, he dismissed a suggestion that Labour has an issue with pensioners: “This is nothing like the winter fuel debate. Nothing like it at all. So the triple lock has taken the basic state pension up, and that’s a really good thing. And by the end of this decade, it will be at record levels, and it will carry on going up under the plan that I mentioned yesterday. But it won’t go up as sharply as it would have done if we had the original triple lock.”
On whether pensioners will lose out, Burnham said: “No, it maintains the pension. The pension will still go up, linked to prices and earnings over the long run, so it will still go up and it will still keep pace. The difference is by moving away from the original triple lock. I can give pensioners a better deal, and you’ll ask me, well, how in those circumstances?
“Because the money that it does release pays for a National Care Service, high quality, person-centred, free personal care in people’s homes. Currently, people are paying care charges from their pension, and that is highly unfair to those pensioners. It’s a much better deal to have a pension that keeps pace with prices, and also a personal care system that gives you peace of mind in later life.”
On a £200 billion plus estimated cost of the new care service, he said: “I’m not sure I recognise that figure, but I think your viewers, to be honest, I think I know them, and maybe they don’t always agree with everything I say, but they want to see the price of electricity come down, and I’m taking VAT off electricity tomorrow.
“They want to see a water system that works in the public interest. I think many of your viewers think the privatisation and breakup of all of those things was actually a mistake in the 80s and 90s.”
Asked if the Makerfield test was alive and well, he said: “Oh, 100%. It’s at the heart of government, and every civil servant knows that.”

British Prime Minister Andy Burnham on Wednesday said there were “strong indications” Iran was involved in suspicious activity at a UK airbase that triggered a major security incident this weekend.
“There are strong indications that Iran played a part in what happened over the weekend at RAF Fairford,” Burnham told the BBC, referring to Sunday’s bomb scare near the airbase in southwest England, which is used by the US military in its war against Iran.
“Of course it remains an ongoing, complex, and serious police investigation,” said Burnham.
Iran’s embassy in London earlier said it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns” speculation it was involved in the incident. Police said on Tuesday that no explosives were found at the scene.
The nature of the threat has not been explained by officials.
Burnham’s comments are the first official confirmation from UK authorities that Iran may have had a hand in the incident, which saw three white vans appearing to head towards RAF Fairford in the early hours of Sunday.
A local resident who rang the police said she saw a group of masked men near the vans, which were blocking a road in a village next to the military base.
Growing confusion
The case was plunged into confusion when UK police released on bail five British men it had arrested on Sunday on suspicion of explosives and terrorism offences.
After three days of investigations, including using a bomb disposal team, police said Tuesday they had found no explosives in the vehicles, but they had retrieved a “quantity of petrol”.
Then on Wednesday, The Times newspaper reported that the incident had been foiled after one of the five suspects tipped off the police before the group was apprehended.
US President Donald Trump and his Secretary of State Marco Rubio had previously indicated that intelligence bodies were aware of the suspects and that a foreign state could be involved, but UK officials had not weighed in.
“We have been waiting to confirm what we could say, but we can now confirm our belief that Iran played a part,” Burnham told Sky News.
Speculation was rife that Iran or another hostile state could have been involved, after Tehran previously warned London against allowing its military bases to be used by Washington.
Britain gave the US the greenlight to use RAF Fairford for defensive strikes against Iran, drawing Tehran’s ire and unease from some residents in the Gloucestershire countryside where the base is located.
